subsection: 3. British withdrawal from Palestine, the origins of the Arab–Israeli conflict and the Suez Crisis, 1956

notes.h: Background: Palestine, Britain's wartime promises and the Mandate
notes.b: Before 1917 Palestine belonged to the Ottoman Empire. Britain's wartime deals about its future pointed in different directions, and that contradiction lies behind much of the later conflict.
points: Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire until Britain captured it in 1917-18, during the First World War. Arabs were the large majority of the population and Jews a small minority.

Britain promised support to the Arabs in the McMahon-Hussein correspondence of 1915-16, between Sir Henry McMahon (British high commissioner in Egypt) and Hussein, sharif of Mecca, so that the Arabs would revolt against the Ottomans. Whether Palestine was included in the promised Arab independence was and is disputed.
In 1916 the Sykes-Picot agreement between Britain and France planned to divide the Ottoman Middle East between them, which sat uneasily with promises of Arab independence.

Britain then issued the Balfour Declaration in 1917, backing a Jewish national home in Palestine. Three wartime commitments therefore pulled in different directions, so Arabs and Zionists could each claim Britain had promised them Palestine.

After the war the Mandate system, set up by the League of Nations (the international organisation of the 1920s), let a victorious power govern a former Ottoman territory on the League's behalf. Britain governed Palestine under it until 1948.
The San Remo conference of April 1920 assigned the Mandate for Palestine to Britain, and the League confirmed it in 1922, so Britain's rule rested on international approval.
notes.tip: Examiners reward the point that Britain made conflicting promises to Arabs, to France and to Zionists. Use McMahon-Hussein, Sykes-Picot and Balfour by name when you argue about Britain's contribution to tensions.

notes.h: Zionism, the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate
notes.b: Zionism supplied the aim of a Jewish homeland, and Britain's Declaration and Mandate gave it official backing. Both set the Jewish national movement against the Arab majority in the same land.
points: Zionism was the movement for a Jewish national homeland in Palestine. It took its political form under Theodor Herzl, who led the first Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897.

The Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917 was a letter from Arthur Balfour, the British foreign secretary, to Lord Rothschild. It said Britain viewed ‘with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people’.

The Declaration added a safeguard: nothing was to be done to prejudice the civil and religious rights of the existing non-Jewish communities. This was a promise to the Arab majority, but it left their political rights unmentioned and contradicted the wartime promises made to the Arabs.

The Mandate for Palestine, granted to Britain, came into force in September 1923. Transjordan, the land east of the River Jordan, was separated from the area west of the river in the early 1920s, so the Mandate then covered Palestine west of the Jordan.
notes.tip: Keep the three documents apart: the Balfour Declaration (1917) supports a national home, the Peel plan (1937) proposes partition and the White Paper (1939) limits immigration. Quote only the short Balfour phrase.

notes.h: Immigration, the Arab Revolt, the Peel plan and the 1939 White Paper
notes.b: As Jewish immigration grew, Arab opposition turned to open revolt. Britain tried partition first and then restriction, and satisfied neither side.
points: Jews were about 11 per cent of Palestine's population in the 1922 census and roughly 30 per cent by 1939. This rise alarmed the Arab majority, who feared losing land and control of their country.
Nazi rule in Germany from 1933 raised Jewish immigration sharply, because Jews were fleeing persecution and Palestine was the place Zionists wanted them to go.
The Arab Revolt of 1936-39 was a rising against Mandate rule and Jewish immigration. British forces put it down. Haj Amin al-Husseini, the Mufti of Jerusalem, was the leading Palestinian Arab figure.

The Peel Commission of 1937 proposed partition into a small Jewish state, an Arab state joined to Transjordan and a British-held enclave including Jerusalem. Arab leaders rejected it, and the British soon dropped it.

The White Paper (a government policy statement) of 17 May 1939 limited Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years, after which it would depend on Arab consent. It also restricted Jewish land purchases and promised an independent Palestine within ten years.
Zionists rejected the White Paper because it closed Palestine to Jews just as persecution in Europe worsened. Many Arabs were also unhappy because it did not go further.
notes.tip: For the essay on how far Britain caused Middle East tensions, use the Mandate's handling of immigration and the 1939 White Paper as points for Britain, and Arab and Jewish nationalism as points against.

notes.h: Key concepts: Zionism, terrorism, Arab nationalism and nationalisation
notes.b: Four terms recur in this topic. Examiners ask for each as a short definition plus an example, so learn a one-line definition for each.
points: Zionism is the movement for a Jewish national homeland in Palestine. Theodor Herzl founded it in its political form, and its first Congress met at Basel in 1897.

Terrorism is violence against civilians or political targets to create fear and advance a political aim. Jewish and Arab groups in Palestine both used it. Examples are the Irgun bombing of the King David Hotel in 1946 and the attack on Deir Yassin in 1948.
Arab nationalism is the movement for Arab independence and unity, opposed to Western control and to the state of Israel. Nasser was its leading figure in the 1950s.
Nationalisation is a government taking over a privately owned business or resource. Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company in 1956, so its profits went to Egypt.
notes.tip: Give a clear one-line definition plus one example for Zionism and for terrorism. For terrorism, define it neutrally and name examples from both sides.

notes.h: The Holocaust, Jewish armed groups and the King David Hotel
notes.b: The Holocaust made the Jewish demand for a state far more urgent. Britain's immigration limits then led some Jewish groups to turn their weapons against British rule.
points: The Holocaust killed about six million Jews in Europe between 1941 and 1945. It intensified the demand for a Jewish state and for refugee admission to Palestine, which Britain's White Paper limits blocked.
The Haganah, founded in 1920, was the main Jewish defence force. It served the Jewish Agency (the body that represented the Jewish community), which David Ben-Gurion led.

The Irgun was formed in 1931 by Revisionist Zionists and led from 1943 by Menachem Begin. Lehi, or the Stern Gang, was a small splinter group founded in 1940 by Avraham Stern. Both attacked British targets.
From October 1945 to mid-1946 the Haganah, Irgun and Lehi co-operated in the Jewish Resistance Movement, so attacks on British forces rose sharply in this period.

On 22 July 1946 the Irgun bombed the south wing of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem, headquarters of the British administration. It killed 91 people, Arabs, Britons and Jews. Britain condemned it and the Haganah distanced itself.
In July 1947 the Irgun hanged two British sergeants in reprisal for the execution of its members, which showed how violent the conflict with British forces had become.
notes.tip: Keep the groups apart: the Haganah was the mainstream force under the Jewish Agency, the Irgun was Revisionist under Begin, and Lehi was the smallest and most extreme. Use the King David Hotel as your example of terrorism.

notes.h: Refugees, the Anglo-American Committee and why Britain withdrew
notes.b: Britain held out against admitting large numbers of refugees, and the cost of doing so grew. By 1947 the government wanted to end a commitment it could not make work.
points: The Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry recommended in April 1946 that 100,000 Jewish refugees be admitted to Palestine. Britain refused to agree without Arab consent, because it feared Arab anger.

In 1947 the ship Exodus carried about 4,500 Holocaust survivors. Britain turned it back and the passengers were returned to Germany. This drew world sympathy for the Zionist cause and damaged Britain's reputation.

Britain kept tens of thousands of troops in Palestine, and holding the country was costly. Attacks on British forces, such as the King David Hotel bombing and the hanging of two sergeants, added to the pressure.

No solution acceptable to both Arabs and Jews could be found, and the United States pressed Britain over the refugee question. Together these reasons explain why Britain decided in 1947 to give up its Mandate.
notes.tip: For why Britain withdrew, list cost, attacks on British forces, the lack of an agreed solution and American pressure over refugees. Four distinct reasons earn more than one repeated.

notes.h: Britain refers Palestine to the United Nations and partition, 1947-48
notes.b: Unable to reconcile Arab and Jewish claims, Britain handed the problem to the United Nations in 1947. The UN's partition plan was rejected by the Arabs, and Britain left the fighting to others.
points: In February 1947 the British government, with Ernest Bevin, announced that it would refer the Palestine question to the United Nations. The UN Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP) recommended partition in 1947, and in September Britain announced that the Mandate would end.

Resolution 181 of the UN General Assembly, passed on 29 November 1947 by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstentions, divided Palestine into an Arab state and a Jewish state, with Jerusalem under international control. Britain abstained.
The plan gave the Jewish state about 55 per cent of the land, although Jews were only about a third of the population. This is why Arabs saw it as unjust.
The United States and the Soviet Union both voted for partition, an unusual agreement in the early Cold War.
The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected partition, and fighting between Arab and Jewish forces began in December 1947.
Britain refused to enforce partition itself, so no authority was left to keep order. The Mandate ended on 14 May 1948, the day Israel was proclaimed.
In the civil war that followed, Jewish forces under Plan Dalet took Tiberias, Haifa and Jaffa in April-May 1948, and most of the Arab inhabitants of these cities fled.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Resolution 181 (partition, November 1947) with Resolution 194 (refugees, December 1948). Know the vote, the terms and who supported and opposed the plan.

notes.b: The Mandate's end and Israel's declaration were followed at once by invasion. The war that began decided the new state's shape and created the refugee problem.
points: David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948 and became prime minister. The United States recognised Israel within minutes, de facto, and the Soviet Union recognised it three days later.

Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon sent forces into Palestine on 15 May 1948, the day after the Mandate ended, and the first Arab-Israeli war began. Israel survived and held more territory than the UN plan gave it.
About 6,000 Israelis died in the war, roughly 1 per cent of the Jewish population, so the new state paid a heavy price for survival.

On 9 April 1948 Irgun and Lehi fighters attacked the village of Deir Yassin near Jerusalem and killed about 100 to 120 villagers, although early reports said 254. Both sides used the attack for propaganda, and it fuelled panic among Arabs.
Four days later Arab forces killed about 78 Jews in a convoy travelling to the Hadassah hospital on Mount Scopus. Deir Yassin and this attack are both examples of terrorism.
notes.tip: Remember the date order: the Mandate ended on 14 May 1948, Israel was declared on 14 May and the Arab armies entered on 15 May.

notes.h: Palestinian refugees, the armistices and consequences for Israel
notes.b: The war left a lasting refugee problem and new borders that no one fully accepted. It also shaped Israel as a state of immigration.
points: About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from what became Israel; estimates range roughly from 600,000 to 750,000. Some left in fear, as after Deir Yassin, and some were driven out.

UN General Assembly Resolution 194 of December 1948 said refugees who wished to return and live in peace should be allowed to. Israel has not accepted a general right of return, so the refugee question stayed unresolved.
The armistice agreements of 1949 ended the fighting without a peace. Jordan held the West Bank, which it annexed in 1950 although few states recognised this, and Egypt administered the Gaza Strip.
Israel's Law of Return of 1950 gave Jews the right to immigrate, which brought large numbers to the new state. Many Jews also left or were pushed out of Arab states after 1948.
notes.tip: On refugees, give about 700,000 with the range, explain both flight and expulsion, and name Resolution 194 and the unresolved right of return.

notes.h: Nasser, Arab nationalism and the road to Suez, 1952-55
notes.b: Nasser took power in Egypt in 1952 and set out to free Egypt from British influence. His clashes with Britain, Israel and the West then led towards the Suez Crisis.
points: The Free Officers overthrew King Farouk on 23 July 1952. Gamal Abdul Nasser became the leading figure, became prime minister in April 1954 and was elected president by referendum in June 1956.
The Anglo-Egyptian Agreement of October 1954 provided for British troops to leave the Suez Canal base, a British military base beside the canal. They had left by June 1956.
Nasser attended the Bandung Conference of Asian and African states in April 1955 and supported anti-colonial movements, so Arab nationalism for him meant opposing Western control.
The Baghdad Pact of 1955 linked Britain, Iraq, Turkey, Iran and Pakistan. Nasser saw it as an attempt to isolate Egypt, so he opposed it.

Egypt barred Israeli ships from the canal and the Straits of Tiran. Fedayeen (Palestinian raiders) attacked Israel from Gaza, and an Israeli raid on Gaza in February 1955 killed 38 people. This pushed Nasser to look for arms.
In 1955 Nasser bought arms from the Soviet bloc through Czechoslovakia. This made Egypt a point of Cold War rivalry, because Western powers now feared Soviet influence in the Middle East.
notes.tip: Nasser's actions are part of the 'against Britain' argument in the tensions essay, so link his arms deal and Arab nationalism to the points about his own responsibility.

notes.h: Aswan High Dam and the nationalisation of the Suez Canal, 1956
notes.b: In 1956 the loss of Western funding for the Aswan High Dam pushed Nasser into a bold response. The canal he seized mattered greatly to Britain and France.
points: Egypt recognised communist China in May 1956. The United States withdrew its offer to finance the Aswan High Dam on 19 July 1956 and Britain followed within days.

The Suez Canal opened in 1869. Britain bought the Khedive's shares, about 44 per cent, in 1875 under Disraeli, and in the 1950s about two-thirds of Western Europe's oil passed through it. It was the sea route between Europe and Asia.

On 26 July 1956 Nasser announced the nationalisation of the Suez Canal Company, the private company that owned the canal. The dam was to be financed from canal revenues, so the nationalisation answered the Western withdrawal.

Anthony Eden, Britain's prime minister, feared for oil supplies and British prestige. Guy Mollet, France's prime minister, blamed Nasser for backing the Algerian rebels. Israel wanted the Tiran blockade ended and the fedayeen raids stopped.
Diplomacy came first, but attempts to negotiate a settlement failed, so the three countries moved to military plans. The Anglo-French plan was called Operation Musketeer.
The Soviet Union later helped to build the dam, so the Aswan project became a symbol of Egypt's turn towards the Soviet bloc.
notes.tip: For why the Suez Crisis happened, give the Aswan Dam withdrawal, then nationalisation, then each country's motive. Do not mix up the Suez Canal Company (the private owner) with the Suez Canal base.

notes.h: The Sèvres plan and the invasion, October-November 1956
notes.b: Britain, France and Israel prepared the attack in secret and gave it a public excuse. The invasion then followed in a set order.
points: The Protocol of Sèvres was signed secretly near Paris on 24 October 1956 by Britain, France and Israel, with Ben-Gurion attending. Israel would attack Sinai; Britain and France would then demand that both sides withdraw and occupy the canal to ‘separate’ the combatants.
This pretext was false, because the attack had been planned together. The secrecy later made the collusion a political scandal, which is why critics at home condemned it.
1. On 29 October Israel invaded Sinai.
2. On 30 October Britain and France issued an ultimatum telling both sides to withdraw about 10 miles from the canal. Israel accepted and Egypt refused.
3. On 31 October the Anglo-French bombing of Egyptian airfields began.
4. On 5 November British and French paratroopers landed at Port Said and Port Fuad, and on 6 November seaborne landings followed.
5. A ceasefire took effect at midnight on 6-7 November, while the Anglo-French force was still advancing down the canal.
notes.tip: Learn the order: Sèvres (24 October, secret), then Israel (29), ultimatum (30), bombing (31), landings (5-6 November), ceasefire (6-7). Israel's attack came first and the Anglo-French ultimatum after it.

notes.h: US and Soviet pressure and the UN, 1956
notes.b: The invasion was stopped by pressure from the two superpowers and by the UN rather than by Egypt's army. Britain, dependent on American support, could not carry on.
points: President Eisenhower of the United States opposed the action. Britain faced a run on the pound (heavy selling of the currency), and the US withheld support at the IMF (the International Monetary Fund) until Britain agreed to withdraw.
Soviet leaders threatened rocket attacks on London and Paris on 5 November, and the Soviet Union supported Egypt in the UN.
Soviet troops crushed the Hungarian rising on 4 November 1956. This weakened the Anglo-French complaint against Soviet behaviour at the UN and made Eisenhower angrier at his allies.

The UN set up the United Nations Emergency Force (UNEF) in November 1956 on the proposal of Lester Pearson, Canada's foreign minister, to supervise the withdrawal. General E. L. M. Burns commanded it.
notes.tip: For why the invasion failed, put American financial pressure first, then the Soviet threat and the UN, and mention Hungary only as a complication.

notes.b: Suez ended in political defeat for Britain and France and a victory for Nasser, although his army had lost. It also moved power in the Middle East to the United States.
points: Eden resigned on 9 January 1957, in ill health and politically discredited, and Harold Macmillan succeeded him. The crisis showed that Britain could not act against American wishes, so Britain became more dependent on the US.

Britain and France lost their position as the main Western powers in the Middle East. The Eisenhower Doctrine of January 1957 pledged US help to Middle Eastern states against communism, so the US took over the role.
Egypt's army was beaten in Sinai, but Nasser kept the canal and became a hero of Arab nationalism. His prestige in the Arab world rose sharply because he had defied Britain, France and Israel.
Egypt blocked the canal with a number of sunken ships. A UN clearance operation reopened it in April 1957, under Egyptian control, and Egypt seized British and French property.
Israel withdrew from Sinai and Gaza by March 1957 after US assurances about the Straits of Tiran, so Israel gained some security. UNEF was stationed on the Sinai frontier.
The Iraqi monarchy, Britain's close ally, was overthrown in July 1958, and Iraq left the Baghdad Pact in 1959. This showed how British influence among Arab states was falling.
notes.tip: Give results for each country: Britain (Eden's resignation, dependence on the US), France and the Anglo-French position, Egypt and Nasser (military defeat but political victory), and Israel (withdrawal, Tiran assurances, UNEF).

notes.b: Ben-Gurion led the Jewish community in Palestine and became the first prime minister of Israel. He was a labour Zionist leader who shaped the state as it was founded.
points: Born David Grün in 1886 in Plonsk in the Russian Empire, he emigrated to Ottoman Palestine in 1906 and became a leader of labour Zionism.
He led the Jewish Agency executive from 1935 and accepted the UN partition plan of 1947 as a first step towards a Jewish state, because a smaller state was better than none.
He was shaped by events: the Holocaust and the White Paper made the need for a state and for a strong army urgent, and the war of 1948 tested the new state.
He proclaimed Israel on 14 May 1948 as a participant and was prime minister in 1948-54 and 1955-63, also holding the defence ministry. He retired for a time to Sde Boker kibbutz.

He created the Israel Defence Forces in May 1948 and ordered the shelling of the Irgun arms ship Altalena in June 1948 to assert a single army. In October 1956 he attended the secret talks at Sèvres with Britain and France.
Contemporaries differed: most Jews saw him as the founder of the state, while Arabs and Palestinians saw him as the architect of a state that displaced them.

Historians of the ‘new history’ school such as Benny Morris argue there was no overall expulsion plan in 1948 but that expulsions took place, including from Lydda and Ramle in July 1948. How far Ben-Gurion approved them is debated.
notes.tip: In a paragraph on Ben-Gurion give birth, the Jewish Agency in 1935, partition acceptance, 14 May 1948 and prime minister, each with its date. For a longer answer add both the founder and the displacement views.

notes.b: Nasser led Egypt from 1952 and became the most important figure of Arab nationalism. The Suez Crisis was the central event of his career.
points: Born on 15 January 1918 in Alexandria, he trained as an army officer and was one of the Free Officers who overthrew King Farouk in 1952.
He was prime minister from 1954 and president from 1956. He pursued land reform and the Aswan High Dam, and nationalised the canal. He formed the United Arab Republic with Syria in 1958-61.
He was shaped by events: the Western arms refusal, the Gaza raid, the Baghdad Pact and the withdrawal of the dam offer each pushed him towards confrontation.
In the Suez Crisis he was a participant. His army was defeated in Sinai, but he survived the attack with control of the canal confirmed.
Eden and some British commentators compared him with Mussolini and Hitler, because he seemed an aggressive dictator, while Arab nationalists saw a hero who had defied the West.
Historians credit him with land reform, the dam and Arab self-confidence. They criticise his one-party rule, the suppression of the Muslim Brotherhood and the defeat of 1967.
He intervened in the Yemeni civil war from 1962 and blocked the Straits of Tiran in 1967. Egypt lost Sinai in the Six-Day War of June 1967.
He offered to resign after the defeat, withdrew the offer after mass demonstrations, and died on 28 September 1970.
notes.tip: For Nasser give birth, the 1952 coup, the offices of 1954 and 1956, and the nationalisation on 26 July 1956. A balanced view with achievements and failings earns top marks.

notes.h: Assessment: British policy in Palestine and Suez
notes.b: Examiners want a judgement about how far Britain caused the troubles of the Middle East and how far its actions succeeded. Use each pair of points to argue both sides.
points: Britain's contribution, limit: the Mandate's contradictory promises, its handling of immigration, the 1939 White Paper and the abrupt withdrawal in 1948 all left a legacy of refugees and hostility.
Britain was not the only cause, because Arab and Jewish nationalism, the Holocaust, the US and UN, Arab rejection of partition and Nasser's own actions also drove events.
Withdrawal, achievement: Britain ended a costly commitment and passed the question to the UN instead of fighting both communities, as the attacks on British forces had become too great.
Withdrawal, limit: the Mandate's conflicting promises to Arabs and Jews were not reconciled, so the 1948 war left refugees and hostility.
Suez, achievement: Israel overran Sinai in days and the Anglo-French force was advancing down the canal before the ceasefire, so the operation was largely successful as far as it went.
Suez, limit: the operation failed politically. The ceasefire was forced by the United States, the Soviet threat and the UN, and the canal remained in Egyptian hands.

Contemporary view: Eden presented the action as a police action to separate Israel and Egypt, while Labour leader Hugh Gaitskell condemned it and Anthony Nutting, a Foreign Office minister, resigned in protest.
Later view: many historians treat Suez as the moment that exposed the end of Britain's great-power pretensions, while others argue that decolonisation was already under way.
notes.tip: Give a clear judgement with points on both sides. For Britain: contradictory promises, immigration, the White Paper, the sudden withdrawal and the Suez collusion. Against: both nationalisms, the Holocaust, the US and UN, Arab rejection and Nasser.

keyTerms.definition: The movement that sought a Jewish national homeland, which in the 1917–48 period centred on Palestine.
The use of violence against civilians or political targets to create fear and advance a political aim, used in Palestine by Jewish and Arab armed groups.
The British statement of 2 November 1917 supporting a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.
The League of Nations system under which Britain administered Palestine from 1923 until 14 May 1948.
The movement for the political unity and independence of Arab peoples, which opposed both Western control and the state of Israel.
The transfer of a privately owned company or asset to state ownership, as in Nasser's takeover of the Suez Canal Company in 1956.
The secret agreement of October 1956 among Britain, France and Israel that set out the military plan for the invasion of Egypt.
The United Nations Emergency Force, set up in November 1956 to supervise the withdrawal of the invading forces and the Sinai frontier.
The main Jewish defence force in Mandate Palestine, founded in 1920 and under the Jewish Agency, which became the core of the Israel Defence Forces.
The Revisionist Zionist armed group, led from 1943 by Menachem Begin, which attacked British and Arab targets including the King David Hotel.
The British policy of May 1939 that limited Jewish immigration and land purchases and promised an independent Palestine in ten years.
The group of Egyptian army officers that overthrew King Farouk in July 1952 and brought Nasser to power.
